title: Parity games in polynomial time
formal: Do there exist a deterministic Turing machine A and constants \(K,c>0\) such that, on every finite parity game G and designated vertex s, A decides whether Even has a winning strategy from s in at most \(K(\mathrm{L}+1)^{c}\) steps, where L is the explicit binary encoding length of \((G,s)\)?
definitions: G consists of a nonempty vertex set \(V=\{1,\ldots ,n\}, a\) directed edge set \(E\subseteq V\times V\) with at least one outgoing edge at every vertex, a partition \(V=V_{\mathrm{Even}}\sqcup V_{\mathrm{Odd}}\), and a priority function \(p:V\to N\). Self-loops are allowed. The input explicitly lists all vertices, edges, owner bits and priorities, with integers in binary and delimiters; \(s\in V\) is included. A play is an infinite sequence \(v_{0}v_{1}\ldots\) with \(v_{0}=s\) and \((v_{i},v_{i+1})\in E\). At a vertex owned by a player that player chooses the next vertex. A strategy maps every finite valid play ending at a vertex owned by that player to a legal successor. Even wins a play if the minimum priority occurring infinitely often is even; Odd wins otherwise. A winning strategy for Even makes every play consistent with it winning for Even, irrespective of Odd’s choices. The algorithm must answer YES exactly when such a strategy exists. Strategies are not part of the input. The number and magnitude of priorities are unrestricted input data; the running-time exponent may not depend on them. The task has perfect information, alternating vertex ownership and no probabilistic transitions.

context_blocks.text: Parity games describe infinite behavior using a finite graph and a priority condition. The question is not how to simulate an infinite play; it is how to decide whether one player can force the eventual recurrence pattern of priorities to favor it. This decision problem underlies central constructions in logical verification and synthesis.

Positional determinacy says that a winning player can choose moves using only the current vertex. Thus finite strategies suffice even though the winning condition concerns an infinite play. Their existence does not by itself give a polynomial-time algorithm for finding or choosing the winning strategy. The problem lies in both NP and coNP, and more precisely in UP and coUP.

Calude and coauthors established a quasipolynomial-time algorithm in 2017. Czerwiński and coauthors proved quasipolynomial lower bounds for separating automata used by a broad collection of such algorithms. That lower bound concerns the specified approach, not arbitrary algorithms for parity games.

A November 2025 preprint by Rick van der Heijden claims a polynomial-time algorithm for the full problem. This review located and inspected the claim but did not independently verify its proof or find an authoritative resolution of its correctness. It must be visible on the card rather than omitted from a statement that the problem is confirmed open.

Suilen and Pérez’s April 2026 paper still describes polynomial-time parity-game solving as a longstanding open question while reducing parity games to a robust-MDP threshold problem. This later usage is evidence about the literature, not a proof that the earlier claim is false. The card therefore carries an explicitly unverified current status while completing the mathematical formulation and preserving its historical identifier.

why: Determine the exact polynomial-time boundary for a central finite representation of infinite game behavior.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation, with the stated model, domains, promises and quantifiers. A conditional theorem settles only its conditional version. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-verified proof matching the full target.

importance.reason: A defining algorithmic question of verification and infinite-duration games, with direct modal-logic and synthesis connections and a major quasipolynomial breakthrough. Its former rank came from a provisional unassessed score, not a low-significance assessment. The score does not certify the correctness or failure of the located solution claim.

sentences: Parity games ask which player can force an infinite play whose minimum infinitely recurring priority has the desired parity.
The target is a uniform deterministic polynomial-time decision algorithm for arbitrary finite arenas and binary-encoded priorities.
Quasipolynomial algorithms and lower bounds for separating-automaton methods are known.
A November 2025 preprint claims a polynomial-time solution, but this review did not establish its correctness.
A separate April 2026 paper still treats the question as open, so the completed card explicitly records an unverified current status.
